questionText:
Read the following excerpt on M.A.R. Chughtai's 'Radhika' and answer the questions that follow:

Created around 1940 by master artist Muhammad Abdur Rahman (M.A.R.) Chughtai, 'Radhika' is a peerless triumph of calligraphic delicacy and wash painting. Tracing his lineage to a celebrated family of imperial Mughal court architects, Chughtai synthesized the Bengal wash technique with the refined linear elegance of Persian and Mughal miniatures and the whiplash curves of Art Nouveau. In 'Radhika', the heroine is depicted walking gracefully away from her chamber carrying a burning earthen lamp (diya) in her hand. Her head is tilted down in modest reverie (lajja), her serene countenance illuminated by the warm golden glow of the flame. Fluttering around the burning wick are moths, visualising the classical Persian and Urdu poetic metaphor of the moth (parwana) selflessly drawn to the flame (shama)—an allegory of Radha's all-consuming, self-surrendering love for Krishna.
